implementation_notes: The standard library supplies kotlin.Result: a value class that is either Success(value) or Failure(Throwable), with fold/onSuccess/onFailure/map/recover and runCatching to capture a throwing block, and since Kotlin 1.5 it may be used as a return type. The failure branch can only hold a Throwable, which is exact when the failure came from an exception and awkward when the reason is a domain value - then a hand-written sealed hierarchy (or Arrow's Either) is the better fit. Prefer fold/onSuccess+onFailure over a when over the value classes, because Result is not a sealed hierarchy and a missing branch is not a compile error.
pitfalls: Failure only holds a Throwable: a domain reason has to become an exception subclass (and the code is exception-shaped again) or move to a sealed hierarchy or Arrow Either.
runCatching catches Throwable, including CancellationException - wrapping suspending code without rethrowing cancellation breaks structured concurrency.
when over Result.Success/Result.Failure is not exhaustiveness-checked, so a forgotten branch yields an unhandled value rather than a compile error; fold forces both handlers.
getOrThrow()/getOrElse { throw ... } reintroduce the exception path; keep them at the edges where the caller genuinely wants the exception channel.

variants.name: Hand-written sealed Either hierarchy
variants.idiom_name: sealed class Either<out L, out R> + exhaustive when
variants.implementation_notes: A hand-written sealed class hierarchy gives the general two-outcome type: Either<out L, out R> with a data class per case, consumed by a when expression whose branches the compiler checks exhaustively - no else arm is required, and adding a case turns every incomplete match into a compile error. Choose it when the reason is a domain type rather than a Throwable, or when the project does not want Arrow; the cost is writing map/flatMap/fold yourself, with the variance annotations that make Either usable in generic positions.
pitfalls: Variance has to be declared deliberately (out parameters plus Nothing for the missing side) or Either<L, R> will not compose in generic positions such as List<Either<E, T>>.
A sealed hierarchy is module-scoped: subclasses must live in the same module and compilation unit set, so clients cannot extend the type - normally what you want, but it rules out third-party cases.
Star-projected or raw Either<*, *> values erase the payload types, so pattern matching still compiles while the reason and value lose their static types.
